paragraphs.heading: Animals without a backbone
paragraphs.text: Invertebrates are animals that never grow a backbone, also called a spine or vertebral column, and do not keep one either. The word comes from Latin: vertebra means a joint, and the prefix in- means "not" or "without". Most animal species are invertebrates, and one estimate puts the share at 97%. They range in size from myxozoans 10 μm across to the colossal squid, at 9–10 m long.

paragraphs.heading: Not a true family tree group
paragraphs.text: Biologists call the group paraphyletic: it takes in every animal except one branch, the vertebrates. Some animals counted as invertebrates, such as the tunicates and the Cephalochordata, are actually closer relatives of vertebrates than of other invertebrates. So the word does not name a real taxon the way Arthropoda or Vertebrata does. It is a term of convenience rather than a branch of the tree of life.

paragraphs.heading: Who belongs
paragraphs.text: Almost all invertebrates fall within one branch, the Protostomia, which holds arthropods, molluscs, annelids and flatworms. Other well-known ones are deuterostomes, such as echinoderms and tunicates, or sit outside that split altogether, such as cnidarians and sponges. Many invertebrate groups have more species, and more varied ones, than all the vertebrates put together. Of the invertebrate species that have been described, insects make up by far the largest number.

paragraphs.heading: Bodies without bone
paragraphs.text: In the older sense of the word, invertebrates have no skeleton of bone, either inside or outside the body. Their body plans differ enormously. Many, like jellyfish and worms, have a skeleton made of fluid, called a hydrostatic skeleton, while others, like insects and crustaceans, have a hard outer shell called an exoskeleton. As animals, they must eat other living things. With a few exceptions, such as the Porifera, their bodies are built of distinct tissues, usually with a digestive chamber that has one or two openings.

paragraphs.heading: Lopsided bodies
paragraphs.text: Most many-celled animals have some kind of symmetry, but a minority have none. All gastropods are asymmetric: snails and sea snails carry coiled shells, and even a slug, which looks even on the outside, has its breathing hole, the pneumostome, on its right side. Fiddler crabs and hermit crabs often have one claw much bigger than the other. If a male fiddler crab loses its big claw, it grows a new one on the opposite side after moulting.

paragraphs.heading: A handy label
paragraphs.text: Vertebrates make up such a small share of all animals that splitting the animal kingdom into vertebrates and invertebrates is of limited practical use. The only thing every invertebrate shares is the missing backbone. That is no more a real biological bond than wings are a reason to group insects, bats and birds together. Even so, the idea has lasted for more than a century, both in everyday speech and among zoologists, as a convenient name for animals that are not vertebrates.
